“Well, you see, it happened dis way. Ole missus—dat’s Miss Watson—she’s forever pickin’ at me, en usin’ me pooty hard, but she awluz promised she wouldn’ sell me down to Orleans. But I seen a slave trader hangin’ roun’ de place a good deal lately, en I got to feelin’ oneasy. Well, one night I crep’ up to de do’ mighty late, en it warn’t shut tight, en I hear ole missus tell de widder she’s gwyne to sell me down to Orleans. She didn’ wish to do it, she said, but dey’d give her eight hund’d dollars for me, en dat wuz too big a heap o’ money for her to stan’ agin. De widder tried to make her promise she wouldn’, but I didn’ stay for what come next. I cleared out mighty fas’, I tell you.

“I started off en scrambled down de hill, thinkin’ I’d steal a skift somewheres on de sho’ above town; but folks wuz still movin’ about, so I crep’ into de ole broken-down cooper-shop by de bank, to wait till dey all went away. Well, I stayed dah de whole night. Somebody wuz always about. Roun’ six in de mawnin’ de skifts started passin’, en by eight er nine everybody in de skifts wuz talkin’ how yo’ pap had come across to town en said you’d been killed. De las’ boats wuz crowded wid ladies en genlmen goin’ across to look at de place. Now en den dey’d stop by de sho’ en rest b’fo’ startin’ over, en from deir talk I learned all about de killin’. I wuz mighty grieved you wuz killed, Huck, but I ain’t grievin’ now.

“I stayed beneath de shavin’s all day. I wuz hungry, but not scared; for I knowed ole missus en de widder meant to leave for de camp-meet’n’ soon after breakfas’, en stay away all day. Dey knows I takes de cattle off about daylight, so dey wouldn’ look for me roun’ home, en wouldn’ miss me till dark dat evenin’. De other servants wouldn’ notice me gone, kase dey’d slip away en take a holiday de minute de ole folks wuz gone.

“Well, arter dark I started up de river road, en walked two mile er better till I come where dey warn’t any houses. I’d settled in my mind what I meant to do. You see, if I kept tryin’ to escape afoot, de dogs could follow me; if I stole a skift en crossed over, dey’d miss de boat, en know pooty near where I’d landed on de other bank, en where dey could find my track.

Do not misunderstand me; I was never truly mad. Even when my tumultuous thoughts seemed to hurry me towards insanity, I remained conscious of my condition, and disclosed them to nothing save solitude and silence. Those about me perceived none of this. They beheld only a poor girl whose spirit was broken, speaking softly and gently, while tears would occasionally escape beneath her lowered eyelids, which she endeavoured to conceal. A girl who sought to be alone and recoiled from notice; who never smiled; ah, no! I did not smile—and that was all.

At last I escaped. I departed from my guardian’s house, and no tidings of me ever followed; the letters I left, together with other circumstances I had contrived, persuaded them that I had taken my own life. Thus the search for me was less diligent than it would otherwise have been, and before long every remembrance and trace of me disappeared. I sailed from London in a little vessel bound for a northern English port. Now that my endeavour had succeeded, and I found myself entirely alone, peace came back to me. The sea lay still, and the ship glided gently onward; sitting on deck beneath heaven’s open canopy, I fancied myself another being. No longer the frantic, raving, most unhappy Mathilda, but a young Hermitess vowed to retirement, whose heart she must labour to preserve from every disturbance and unhallowed despair. The fanciful habit, resembling a nun’s, which I had assumed; the thought that my existence itself was a secret belonging to me alone; the solitude appointed for all my future days, fostered mild thoughts within my injured heart. The air stirring through my hair renewed my strength, and with peaceful eyes I observed the sunlight sparkling upon the waves, and the birds pursuing one another above the water, barely touching it with their feathers. My sleep, too, was free of troubled dreams; I woke restored, to taste once more the quiet of my liberty.

Four days brought us to the harbour for which we had sailed. Unwilling to settle upon the coast, I travelled inland at once. I had already determined the kind of place in which I should dwell. It must be a lonely house upon an extensive plain, remote from any other dwelling: a place where the entire horizon lay before me, and where I might roam a long way untroubled by the appearance of another human being. I bore mankind no hatred, but felt that the peaceful course of my emotions required solitude. I established myself amid a broad waste, upon a desolate heath scattered with stones, between which grew short grass, with a few rushes here and there beside some little pool.

Words cannot express the transport with which I turned from the political quarrels of my country, and the bodily sufferings of far-off lands, towards my dear home, that chosen dwelling of kindness and affection; towards peace and the exchange of every hallowed sympathy. If I had never left Windsor, I could not have felt these things so keenly; but in Greece I had fallen a prey to dread and lamentable change; there, following a season of sorrow and anxiety, I had witnessed the departure of two whose very names stood for virtue and greatness. Yet griefs like these could never penetrate the family circle still remaining to me, whilst we lived quietly, withdrawn within our cherished forest. The advance of years did indeed work some slight alteration here; and time, according to its custom, impressed the signs of mortality upon our hopes and enjoyments. Idris, that most loving wife, sister, and friend, was also a fond and gentle mother. Motherhood was to her no diversion, as it is to many, but a passion. Three children had been born to us; the second had died during my stay in Greece. That loss had mingled sorrow and apprehension with the victorious ecstasies of maternal love. Until then, these small creatures born of her, the youthful inheritors of her fleeting existence, had seemed assured of life; now she feared that the merciless destroyer might carry off her surviving treasures as it had taken their brother. Their slightest sickness wrung her with terror; any separation from them made her wretched. She had stored all her happiness in their frail lives, and maintained an endless vigil lest the stealthy thief should again rob her of these precious jewels. Happily, there was little to justify her alarm. Alfred, who was now nine, was an honest, manly little boy, with a bright forehead, tender eyes, and a disposition at once gentle and independent. Our youngest remained an infant; yet the bloom of health coloured his soft cheek, and his tireless liveliness made our rooms ring with harmless laughter.

Clara was past that age whose speechless ignorance awakened Idris’s fears. She was beloved by Idris and by us all. Intelligence blended in her so happily with innocence, feeling with patience, gravity with unclouded good temper; such surpassing beauty accompanied such winning simplicity, that among our possessions she rested like a pearl within a shrine, a treasure of excellence and wonder.

As winter began, our Alfred, now nine years old, went for the first time to school at Eton. To him this seemed the earliest stride towards manhood, and his pleasure answered to that belief. Sharing studies and diversions brought out his finest qualities: his constant perseverance, his generosity, and his firmness under good command.
